I've noticed some threads where one person has deleted all their posts, leaving only one side of (what appeared to be) a relevant and interesting discussion. I suspect the comments where deleted because the author realized their position was incorrect and didn't want to be associated with it anymore, which is understandable. Unfortunately, it deprives everyone else of the ability to learn what the author had.

Therefore, I propose a Disown feature as an alternative to the Delete feature: The author of the comment will be removed from the comment but the comment itself will stay. It can still collect voats like a normal comment but they will not affect the original author.

This way, an errant user can distance themselves from their mistakes without also undoing all the work put into the discussion.
A Disown Comment feature, to alleviate all the [deleted] posts

This is one of the best original ideas I've ever heard for a platform like this. Second.

You frequently see deleted comments with 50+ replies, and if no one quotes it you never know what the hell happened. People are to precious about their points, but they're necessary to motivate people to participate.

This is an excellent idea. However, how will the system deal with up/downvoats? Are the comments still voatable? If not, they may quickly find their way to the land of never-seen-comments, which is not what we want. But if the they are still voatable, does the author get the points or do they float into oblivion?

Just a few thoughts on how this would be implemented.
The comments would collect upvoats/downvoats and sort like regular comments, they would just be isolated to that specific comment and wouldn't affect the original poster positively or negatively.
I wonder if this anonymous commenting process might be a boon to malicious individuals.
From a malicious standpoint, it could be used similar to a throwaway account. I don't think it would make much difference though, since it's so easy to register a new account here.

Microsoft Surface Pro 3

Windows 8.1 is enormously fantastic for touch devices, and has had fantastic handwriting support for over a decade now. OneNote is far and away a killer app for Microsoft in the tablet market, and can be found for free in the app stores of each ecosystem. This doesn't really do much for selling the Surface specifically, so I'll work more on that now.

Unlike the iPad or Android tablets, the Surface (not-RT, mind you) isn't a very large phone running a phone operating system; it's a full-fledged computer running the exact same Windows as desktops and laptops. They come with PC-level specs, such as 4GB of RAM, >100GB SSDs, and Intel i3–i7 processors, and still have terrific battery life (I stretch mine for ten-hour days of class very easily, doing both note-taking and running more expensive programs), have very high quality (not Retina, but, not far shy) screens and touch reception, and Windows' handwriting support and general touch/writing interface is marvelous. The keyboards for them are also very nice -- I have both a purely-touch keyboard, which is okay but I still prefer the mechanical one. The touch keyboard doesn't have any physical cues for where the keys are or whether you've actually gotten a press registered, so you do have to look at it or get very good at touch-typing, but it has yet to have issues registering my presses. The mechanical keyboard has stood up to lots of use and still works perfectly. The fact that the keyboards magnetically seek their attachment point (as does the power cord) is also very nice, as is the fact that the keyboards are also covers that protect the screen when folded shut and can take a fair amount of abuse without damage.

Downside, of course, is that they're expensive, because as stated you're buying a laptop that happens to be in a nicely mobile form factor, not a phone that got scaled up. They also only have one USB port on them, though there is a docking station if you are in a position to use it as a desktop computer. The only monitor-out port is a mini-DisplayPort (I believe?) though adapters to VGA, HDMI, and (I believe) DVI also exist, as does Microsoft's answer to the ChromeCast whose name I can't for the life of me remember but unlike the ChromeCast shows up as an actual monitor to the OS, not an option individual programs have to implement.

If you're already in the Windows ecosystem, then a Surface will fit in perfectly, especially if you sign into other devices with a Microsoft account – themes, settings, stored usernames/passwords all synchronize so once you're signed in there's very little required to feel already at home.

I've never used an Android tablet, but, if being able to use handwriting or Windows desktop programs are at all sticking points for you, this is your best option and, in my opinion, the only sane one.
